# Core ML Models

This chapter is a compact comparison map for classical models: their assumptions, decision boundaries, failure modes, and appropriate baselines.

## Linear and logistic regression

### Q: What is multicollinearity? {#q-multicollinearity .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Multicollinearity occurs when one or more predictor variables are approximately linear combinations of others. In linear regression this makes the coefficients poorly identified: predictions may remain reasonable, while individual coefficient estimates can become highly unstable.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Intuition

Suppose two predictors satisfy

$$
x_2 \approx 2x_1.
$$

Then a linear model produces

$$
\hat y
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2
\approx \beta_0+(\beta_1+2\beta_2)x_1.
$$

The data may identify the combined effect $\beta_1+2\beta_2$, but provide little information about how that effect should be divided between the two coefficients. If the dependence were exact, replacing $(\beta_1,\beta_2)$ by $(\beta_1+2c,\beta_2-c)$ would leave every fitted value unchanged.

This is why different samples can produce very different coefficients—even opposite signs—while producing nearly identical predictions.

#### Mathematical View

For the linear model

$$
y=X\beta+\varepsilon,
$$

ordinary least squares gives

$$
\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y
$$

when $X$ has full column rank. Exact linear dependence makes $X^\top X$ singular, so coefficients are not unique. Approximate dependence makes it ill-conditioned, so inversion magnifies small changes in the sample or labels.

Under the classical assumptions

$$
E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma^2I,
$$

the coefficient covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)
=\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}.
$$

If

$$
X^\top X=Q\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)Q^\top,
$$

then the variance in eigenvector direction $q_k$ is $\sigma^2/d_k$. A small eigenvalue therefore creates a weakly identified, high-variance coefficient direction.

The spectral condition number is

$$
\kappa_2(X^\top X)
=\frac{d_{\max}}{d_{\min}}
=\left(\frac{s_{\max}(X)}{s_{\min}(X)}\right)^2.
$$

A large condition number means some directions are much less identified than others, so perturbations can be strongly amplified. Put columns on comparable scales before interpreting it.

#### Common Mistakes

- Multicollinearity does not automatically imply poor predictions.
- A large pairwise correlation is one possible symptom, not the definition; dependence can involve several variables.
- Unstable coefficients do not by themselves show that a feature has no predictive value.
- Scaling makes a condition number interpretable but cannot remove a genuine linear dependence.
:::
</details>

### Q: Why does multicollinearity increase the variance of regression coefficients? {#q-multicollinearity-coefficient-variance .qa-card}

**Short answer:** When predictors are nearly linearly dependent, $X^\top X$ has very small eigenvalues. Its inverse therefore has very large eigenvalues in those directions, and because $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)=\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}$, small changes in the data can produce large changes in the estimated coefficients.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Math

Assume

$$
y=X\beta+\varepsilon,
\qquad
E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma^2I,
$$

and that $X$ has full column rank. Substituting into the OLS estimator gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\beta
&=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top(X\beta+\varepsilon)\\
&=\beta+(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $E[\hat\beta\mid X]=\beta$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)
&=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)
X(X^\top X)^{-1}\\
&=\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now let

$$
X^\top X=QDQ^\top,
\qquad
D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_p).
$$

For an eigenvector $q_k$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(q_k^\top\hat\beta\mid X)
=\frac{\sigma^2}{d_k}.
$$

Near-collinearity means some nonzero $q_k$ satisfies $Xq_k\approx0$, so

$$
d_k=q_k^\top X^\top Xq_k=\lVert Xq_k\rVert_2^2
$$

is small. The data barely constrain movement in that coefficient direction. For an individual coefficient,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j\mid X)
=\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^p\frac{q_{jk}^2}{d_k},
$$

so the small eigenvalue most strongly destabilizes coefficients whose coordinate axes overlap with its eigenvector.

#### Bias–Variance Connection

Under these assumptions, OLS remains conditionally unbiased; multicollinearity primarily raises variance rather than introducing bias. This is a concrete instance of the variance term in the [bias–variance decomposition](02-generalization-regularization.qmd#q-bias-variance).

The formulas condition on the observed design $X$ and vary the outcome noise, whereas the general learning-theory decomposition usually varies the entire training dataset. Both capture the same practical issue: a weakly identified learning procedure can change substantially when its sample changes. Ridge deliberately introduces bias to reduce this variance.

#### Follow-ups

- Which coefficient combinations become unstable? Those aligned with small-eigenvalue directions of $X^\top X$.
- Can more observations help? Yes if they add information in the weak direction; repeating the same exact feature relationship cannot restore identifiability.
- Why can coefficient signs change across bootstrap samples? Several allocations of a shared effect fit nearly equally well, so sampling noise can move the solution substantially along the weak direction.
:::
</details>

### Q: Does multicollinearity necessarily hurt prediction accuracy? {#q-multicollinearity-prediction .qa-card}

**Short answer:** No. Multicollinearity can make individual coefficients unstable while predictions remain accurate, especially when test data preserve the same feature relationships as training data. It becomes more dangerous under distribution shift, extrapolation, small samples, or sufficiently large estimation variance.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Intuition

If $x_2\approx2x_1$, the data mostly need the model to estimate the combined effect $\beta_1+2\beta_2$. They may contain little evidence about the individual coefficients, but many coefficient pairs can still produce nearly the same fitted values.

With exact dependence, OLS coefficients are not unique, yet the projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$—and therefore the training fitted values—is unique. Near dependence gives the approximate version of this result.

#### Mathematical View

For a new feature vector $x_*$, the estimated conditional mean is

$$
\hat y_*=x_*^\top\hat\beta.
$$

Under the classical OLS assumptions,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_*\mid X,x_*)
=\sigma^2x_*^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}x_*.
$$

Using $X^\top X=Q\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)Q^\top$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_*\mid X,x_*)
=\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^p
\frac{(q_k^\top x_*)^2}{d_k}.
$$

A small $d_k$ creates high predictive variance only when $x_*$ has a component in the corresponding weakly identified direction. If deployment examples preserve the training relationship, they may have little component there, so prediction remains stable even though $\hat\beta$ is unstable. Predicting a fresh observed outcome rather than its conditional mean adds irreducible noise under this model.

#### When Prediction Suffers

- **Correlation structure shifts:** training had $x_2\approx2x_1$, but deployment does not.
- **The model must extrapolate:** new points expose coefficient directions that training barely constrained.
- **The sample is small or noisy:** weak directions have still higher uncertainty.
- **Several directions are poorly identified:** uncertainty affects more of the deployment feature space.
- **Feature availability changes:** losing one member of a redundant group can expose an unstable coefficient allocation.

#### Common Mistakes

Do not remove a variable solely because it is correlated with another. For prediction, compare validated performance, stability under plausible shifts, and operational feature availability. For coefficient interpretation or causal estimation, weak identification is a more direct concern.
:::
</details>

### Q: How would you detect multicollinearity? {#q-detect-multicollinearity .qa-card}

**Short answer:** I would combine domain inspection with pairwise correlations, per-feature VIFs, and singular values or a condition number computed after appropriate scaling. Correlations find simple pairs, VIF detects whether one feature is explained by all the others, and the SVD directly reveals weak directions in the full design matrix.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Correlation Matrix

A correlation matrix is a fast first diagnostic for strongly related pairs, but it cannot detect every multivariable dependence. For example, let $x_1$ and $x_2$ be independent standardized variables and define

$$
x_3=\frac{x_1+x_2}{\sqrt{2}}+\text{small noise}.
$$

Then $x_3$ is nearly determined by $x_1$ and $x_2$, but its pairwise correlations with them are only about $1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.71$. A rule that flags only correlations above $0.9$ would miss the dependence.

#### Variance Inflation Factor

Regress feature $x_j$ on all the other predictors and obtain $R_j^2$. Its variance inflation factor is

$$
\operatorname{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.
$$

If the remaining predictors explain almost all variation in $x_j$, then $R_j^2$ is close to one and little residual variation remains for estimating the unique contribution of $x_j$.

Warnings such as $\operatorname{VIF}>5$ or $\operatorname{VIF}>10$ are heuristics, not mathematical decision boundaries. Their importance depends on sample size, noise, and whether the task values coefficient interpretation or prediction.

#### VIF Math

Assume the predictors are centered and the model includes an intercept. Let

$$
\operatorname{SST}_j
=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2.
$$

Regressing $x_j$ on the other predictors leaves residual sum of squares

$$
\operatorname{SSE}_j
=(1-R_j^2)\operatorname{SST}_j.
$$

Only this residualized part of $x_j$ identifies $\beta_j$. Under homoskedastic errors,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j\mid X)
=
\frac{\sigma^2}
{(1-R_j^2)\sum_i(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2}.
$$

Without linear association with the other centered predictors, the variance would be $\sigma^2/\operatorname{SST}_j$. Their ratio is exactly $1/(1-R_j^2)$, which explains the name VIF.

#### Singular Values and Condition Number

For a centered and appropriately scaled design matrix,

$$
X=USV^\top,
\qquad
S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_p).
$$

A very small singular value means some feature combination $v_k$ satisfies $Xv_k\approx0$. Useful global diagnostics are

$$
\kappa_2(X)=\frac{s_{\max}}{s_{\min}}
$$

and

$$
\kappa_2(X^\top X)=\frac{s_{\max}^2}{s_{\min}^2}.
$$

The corresponding right singular vector identifies the weak combination; an exact zero singular value indicates rank deficiency. Standardize comparable numeric predictors and handle the intercept separately because different units alone can create a large condition number.

#### Practical Workflow

1. Check duplicated columns, deterministic transformations, one-hot encodings, and the dummy-variable trap.
2. Inspect correlations for obvious redundancy.
3. Use VIF when individual coefficient interpretation matters.
4. Use the SVD or condition number for higher-order dependencies.
5. Refit across folds or bootstrap samples to inspect coefficient stability.
6. Decide whether the instability matters for the actual objective; a diagnostic is not an automatic instruction to delete a feature.
:::
</details>

### Q: What would you do if you discover multicollinearity? {#q-handle-multicollinearity .qa-card}

**Short answer:** I would first decide whether the goal is prediction, coefficient interpretation, or causal estimation. I might remove or combine genuinely redundant variables, collect data with more independent variation, use PCA, or apply ridge regression for stability. I would not automatically delete correlated features when validated prediction is already reliable.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Decision Framework

- **Prediction:** keep useful correlated features if held-out performance and plausible-shift tests are stable; ridge is often a strong default.
- **Coefficient interpretation:** decide which effects must be separated, then use domain knowledge to remove, combine, or redesign measurements.
- **Causal estimation:** do not drop a correlated confounder merely to reduce VIF; the estimand and identification assumptions determine the adjustment set.
- **Accidental dependence:** fix duplicated features, deterministic transformations, encoding errors, or leakage in the data pipeline.

#### Remedies

- **Remove a redundant variable** when two features encode essentially the same information and one is cheaper, noisier, less available, or less interpretable.
- **Combine variables** when a domain-motivated aggregate is more meaningful than separate coefficients.
- **Use PCA or dimensionality reduction** to replace correlated features with orthogonal components. This can stabilize estimation but weakens interpretation, and PCA does not use $y$ when choosing directions.
- **Collect more informative data** that varies the correlated features independently. More rows with the same exact dependence do not restore identifiability.
- **Use ridge regression** to shrink weakly identified directions.
- **Use domain-driven feature choice** rather than deleting variables solely because a numerical threshold was crossed.

#### Ridge Math

After centering the predictors and response so that $\beta$ contains only slope coefficients, ridge solves

$$
\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}
=
\arg\min_\beta
\left\{
\lVert y-X\beta\rVert_2^2
+\lambda\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2
\right\},
$$

giving

$$
\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}
=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.
$$

Predictors are usually standardized. If an intercept is fitted explicitly, it is handled separately and is usually not penalized. If

$$
X^\top X
=Q\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)Q^\top,
$$

then ridge shifts every penalized eigenvalue from $d_i$ to $d_i+\lambda$. Its inverse uses $1/(d_i+\lambda)$ instead of $1/d_i$, preventing extremely small-eigenvalue directions from exploding.

Under

$$
y=X\beta+\varepsilon,
\qquad
E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma^2I,
$$

$$
E[\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}\mid X]
=
Q\operatorname{diag}\left(
\frac{d_i}{d_i+\lambda}
\right)Q^\top\beta,
$$

so ridge introduces bias. Its covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}\mid X)
=
\sigma^2Q\operatorname{diag}\left(
\frac{d_i}{(d_i+\lambda)^2}
\right)Q^\top.
$$

Compared with the OLS directional variance $\sigma^2/d_i$, ridge can greatly reduce variance when $d_i$ is small. This is the mathematical bias–variance trade-off behind its stability. See also [L2 regularization and weight decay](02-generalization-regularization.qmd#q-weight-decay).

#### LASSO and Correlated Predictors

LASSO can produce a sparse model, but among predictors carrying similar information it may select one somewhat arbitrarily. Small sample changes can therefore change which feature is retained. That can be acceptable when sparsity is the operational objective, but it is not reliable evidence that the selected feature is uniquely important. Elastic net can be more stable because it combines L1 sparsity with L2 shrinkage.

#### Follow-ups

- Does ridge solve exact multicollinearity? For $\lambda>0$, it makes the penalized system invertible, but the estimator is biased and depends on the penalty.
- How should $\lambda$ be selected? With validation or cross-validation using a metric and split structure that match deployment.
- Does standardization fix multicollinearity? No; it removes scale artifacts and makes regularization comparable across features.
- Should every feature with high VIF be removed? No; VIF measures coefficient-variance inflation, not predictive uselessness or causal irrelevance.
- Can more data solve the problem? Only if the new data add information in the weak directions.
:::
</details>

## Bagging, boosting, and gradient boosting {#sec-boosting-core}


### Q: What is boosting? {#q-boosting .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Boosting builds a strong predictor by adding weak learners sequentially. Each new learner is trained in response to the errors of the current ensemble, and the final predictor is an additive combination of all learners.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Intuition

Instead of asking one complicated model to solve the whole problem, boosting builds the solution incrementally.

A generic boosted model looks like

$$
F_M(x)
=
F_0(x)
+
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
\alpha_m h_m(x).
$$

The first learner captures an easy pattern. The next learner focuses on what remains wrong. Later learners make progressively finer corrections.

This is why very simple base learners, such as shallow decision trees, can combine into a highly expressive model.

#### How It Works

At round $m$:

1. Start with the current ensemble $F_{m-1}$.
2. Determine what the ensemble is currently getting wrong.
3. Fit a weak learner $h_m$ to make a useful correction.
4. Add that learner to the ensemble:

$$
F_m(x)
=
F_{m-1}(x)
+
\alpha_m h_m(x).
$$

Different boosting algorithms differ mainly in how they define the "correction":

- AdaBoost changes example weights.
- Gradient boosting follows loss gradients.
- XGBoost uses gradients, curvature, and explicit tree regularization.

#### Why It Matters

Boosting is especially important for structured/tabular data.

Its key idea is broader than any particular implementation:

> Turn many limited learners into a strong model by correcting errors sequentially.

#### Common Mistakes

- Boosting is not one specific algorithm.
- A weak learner does not mean a useless learner.
- Boosting is not restricted to classification.
- More boosting rounds do not automatically improve test performance.

:::

</details>


### Q: What is the difference between bagging and boosting? {#q-bagging-vs-boosting .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Bagging trains multiple learners largely independently and averages them, mainly reducing variance. Boosting trains learners sequentially, with each learner responding to the current ensemble, allowing it to correct systematic errors more aggressively.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Comparison

| Property | Bagging | Boosting |
|---|---|---|
| Learner training | Largely independent | Sequential |
| Main idea | Average unstable learners | Repeatedly correct errors |
| Typical effect | Strong variance reduction | Often reduces bias and can affect variance |
| Parallelism | Easy across learners | Rounds depend on previous rounds |
| Noise robustness | Often relatively robust | Can be more sensitive |
| Canonical example | Random Forest | AdaBoost / Gradient Boosting / XGBoost |

#### Intuition

Suppose individual decision trees are unstable: slightly changing the training set produces very different trees.

Bagging says:

> Train many different trees and average away their instability.

Boosting instead says:

> Look at what the current ensemble still gets wrong and train another learner specifically to improve it.

These solve different problems.

#### Bias–Variance View

Averaging $M$ estimators with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$ gives approximately

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar f)
=
\sigma^2
\left[
\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{M}
\right].
$$

This explains why bagging benefits from having diverse learners.

Boosting is less naturally described as pure averaging. It changes the fitting problem at every round and can reduce systematic error that a single learner cannot capture.

#### Practical View

Random Forest is often:

- robust,
- easy to tune,
- easy to parallelize,
- a strong baseline.

Boosted trees often achieve stronger tuned performance on tabular problems but usually require more careful regularization and validation.

:::

</details>


### Q: How does AdaBoost work, and why does it upweight mistakes? {#q-adaboost-core .qa-card}

**Short answer:** AdaBoost repeatedly fits weak classifiers on a weighted training set. Misclassified examples receive relatively more weight in the next round, while better weak learners receive larger votes in the final ensemble.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Algorithm

For binary labels

$$
y_i\in\{-1,+1\},
$$

AdaBoost begins with equal example weights.

At round $m$:

1. Fit weak learner $h_m$ using the current weights.
2. Compute its weighted error $\epsilon_m$.
3. Give it vote

$$
\alpha_m
=
\frac12
\log
\left(
\frac{1-\epsilon_m}{\epsilon_m}
\right).
$$

4. Update example weights:

$$
w_i^{(m+1)}
\propto
w_i^{(m)}
\exp
\left(
-\alpha_m y_i h_m(x_i)
\right).
$$

The final classifier uses

$$
F_M(x)
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
\alpha_m h_m(x).
$$

#### Why Mistakes Get More Weight

For a correct prediction,

$$
y_i h_m(x_i)=+1,
$$

so its weight is multiplied by

$$
e^{-\alpha_m}.
$$

For an incorrect prediction,

$$
y_i h_m(x_i)=-1,
$$

so its weight is multiplied by

$$
e^{\alpha_m}.
$$

When $\epsilon_m<0.5$, we have $\alpha_m>0$, so mistakes become relatively more important.

#### Interpretation

The algorithm is effectively saying:

> The current learner already handles these easy examples. Make the next learner pay more attention to what is still difficult.

The vote $\alpha_m$ also gives better weak learners more influence in the final prediction.

#### Common Mistakes

- AdaBoost does not simply train on "the mistakes"; it changes their relative weights.
- The weights encode difficulty accumulated over previous rounds.
- Persistent mislabeled examples can acquire excessive influence.
- The full derivation of the $\alpha_m$ formula is deeper material; the main interview-level point is what the formula means.

:::

</details>


### Q: Why can weak learners combine into a strong learner? {#q-boosting-weak-learners .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Each weak learner only needs to provide a useful correction to the current ensemble. If successive learners make complementary improvements, their weighted sum can form a much richer decision function than any individual learner.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Intuition

Imagine decision stumps.

One stump might correctly separate most examples using $x_1$.

A second stump handles a region where the first stump fails using $x_2$.

A third corrects another remaining region.

The final predictor

$$
F(x)
=
\alpha_1h_1(x)
+
\alpha_2h_2(x)
+
\alpha_3h_3(x)
+\cdots
$$

can represent a much more complicated boundary than any stump individually.

#### AdaBoost View

For AdaBoost, a useful weak learner has weighted error

$$
\epsilon_m<\frac12.
$$

Then

$$
\alpha_m>0.
$$

So each better-than-chance learner contributes in the useful direction.

The important requirement is not that a learner be globally powerful. It must continue to find some useful signal under the changing weighted distribution.

#### Margin View

For binary classification, define the signed margin

$$
y_iF(x_i).
$$

A positive margin means the ensemble classifies the example correctly.

Boosting can progressively increase these margins by accumulating many individually modest corrections.

#### Important Qualification

Weak learners do not magically become strong.

Boosting can fail when:

- the base learner cannot find useful corrections;
- labels contain substantial noise;
- the weak-learning assumption breaks down;
- later rounds mostly fit noise.

:::

</details>


### Q: What is gradient boosting, and why does it fit residuals? {#q-gradient-boosting-core .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Gradient boosting repeatedly adds a weak learner that approximates the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions. For squared-error loss, that negative gradient is exactly the ordinary residual.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Intuition

Suppose the current model predicts

$$
F(x_i).
$$

Ask:

> In which direction should this prediction move to reduce the loss fastest?

The answer is the negative derivative

$$
r_i
=
-
\frac{\partial \ell(y_i,F(x_i))}
{\partial F(x_i)}.
$$

Gradient boosting trains a weak learner to predict these desired corrections.

#### Why Residuals Appear

For squared loss,

$$
\ell(y,F)
=
\frac12(y-F)^2.
$$

Then

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial F}
=
F-y.
$$

Therefore,

$$
-
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial F}
=
y-F.
$$

But

$$
y-F
$$

is exactly the residual.

So "fit a tree to the residuals" is not an arbitrary trick.

It is gradient descent for squared-error loss.

#### Beyond Squared Error

For another differentiable loss, the negative gradient will generally not equal $y-F$.

The targets fitted by the next learner are therefore called **pseudo-residuals**.

This lets gradient boosting support many objectives:

- regression,
- binary classification,
- multiclass classification,
- ranking,
- robust losses.

#### Common Mistakes

- Gradient boosting does not always fit ordinary residuals.
- Residual fitting is the squared-loss special case.
- The weak learner approximates the desired gradient direction; it usually cannot reproduce an arbitrary update perfectly.

:::

</details>


### Q: Why is gradient boosting described as gradient descent in function space? {#q-gradient-boosting-function-space .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Ordinary gradient descent updates a parameter vector. Gradient boosting instead updates the prediction function itself, adding a weak learner that approximates the negative loss gradient across the training examples.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Ordinary Gradient Descent

For parameters $\theta$,

$$
\theta_m
=
\theta_{m-1}
-
\eta
\nabla_\theta L(\theta_{m-1}).
$$

The object being optimized is a finite-dimensional parameter vector.

#### Function-Space View

Gradient boosting considers empirical risk

$$
R(F)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\ell(y_i,F(x_i)).
$$

At the current function $F_{m-1}$, compute

$$
r_{im}
=
-
\left.
\frac{\partial \ell(y_i,F(x_i))}
{\partial F(x_i)}
\right|_{F=F_{m-1}}.
$$

Ideally, we would directly change every prediction in this direction.

But boosting restricts the update to functions representable by the weak-learner class $\mathcal H$.

So it fits

$$
h_m
\approx
r_m
$$

and updates

$$
F_m(x)
=
F_{m-1}(x)
+
\eta \gamma_m h_m(x).
$$

#### Key Insight

The weak learner is playing a role analogous to a gradient direction.

But because only certain functions are available, boosting finds a usable approximation to the ideal negative-gradient update.

That is the meaning of **gradient descent in function space**.

#### Research-Level Takeaway

This viewpoint unifies many apparently different boosting algorithms.

Instead of memorizing "fit residuals," remember:

> Choose a loss, compute how predictions should change to reduce that loss, approximate that change using a weak learner, and add the correction.

:::

</details>


### Q: What is XGBoost, and why does it use both gradients and Hessians? {#q-xgboost-core .qa-card}

**Short answer:** XGBoost is a regularized gradient-boosted-tree method that uses both first- and second-order derivatives of the loss. Gradients indicate which way predictions should move, while Hessians describe local curvature and help determine how large those updates should be.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Conceptual Hierarchy

Think of the relationship as

$$
\text{Boosting}
\supset
\text{Gradient Boosting}
\supset
\text{XGBoost}.
$$

- **Boosting:** sequential additive learning.
- **Gradient boosting:** corrections follow loss gradients.
- **XGBoost:** regularized boosted trees using first- and second-order information plus an optimized training system.

#### Gradient and Hessian

For example $i$,

$$
g_i
=
\frac{\partial \ell}
{\partial \hat y_i},
$$

and

$$
h_i
=
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}
{\partial \hat y_i^2}.
$$

Locally, the change in loss from an update $f(x_i)$ can be approximated by

$$
g_i f(x_i)
+
\frac12 h_i f(x_i)^2.
$$

The gradient gives the preferred direction.

The Hessian tells us about curvature, making the update Newton-like rather than purely first-order.

#### What XGBoost Adds

Beyond the second-order approximation, XGBoost includes ideas such as:

- explicit tree-complexity penalties;
- leaf-score regularization;
- shrinkage;
- row subsampling;
- feature subsampling;
- sparse/missing-value handling;
- efficient split construction.

#### What You Should Know for the Main Interview

You should be able to explain:

- why XGBoost is still gradient boosting;
- why it uses curvature;
- how regularization enters;
- why it is powerful for tabular data.

The full leaf-weight and split-gain derivations belong in deeper boosting material.

:::

</details>


### Q: How do you regularize and tune boosted trees, and when can boosting fail? {#q-boosting-regularization .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Boosted trees are controlled jointly through learning rate, number of trees, tree complexity, subsampling, regularization, and early stopping. Small steps with appropriately limited trees often generalize well, while excessive capacity, noisy labels, or too many rounds can cause the ensemble to fit noise.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Main Controls

**Learning rate**

$$
F_m
=
F_{m-1}
+
\eta h_m.
$$

Smaller $\eta$ makes each correction more conservative but generally requires more trees.

**Number of trees**

Too few can underfit.

Too many can eventually fit noise, especially without shrinkage or early stopping.

**Tree depth**

Shallow trees capture simple interactions.

Deeper trees capture higher-order interactions but increase effective capacity.

**Subsampling**

Using subsets of rows or features introduces randomness and can reduce correlation and overfitting.

**Regularization**

Modern boosted-tree systems can penalize:

- leaf weights;
- number of leaves;
- minimum leaf statistics;
- overly complicated splits.

#### Learning Rate vs Number of Trees

These should be tuned together.

A smaller learning rate with more boosting rounds often works better than a large learning rate with very few trees, but an extremely small rate can be wasteful or underfit under a fixed compute budget.

#### Failure Modes

Boosting can struggle with:

- mislabeled data;
- severe outliers;
- tiny datasets with aggressive tuning;
- overly deep trees;
- excessive boosting rounds;
- train/validation distribution mismatch;
- objectives that do not match the final business metric.

#### Practical Diagnostic

If training error keeps falling while validation error begins rising:

- reduce effective capacity;
- use early stopping;
- increase regularization;
- reduce tree depth;
- increase data;
- introduce subsampling;
- inspect noisy or mislabeled examples.

:::

</details>


### Q: Random Forest vs Gradient Boosting/XGBoost — when would you choose each? {#q-random-forest-vs-boosting .qa-card}

**Short answer:** Random Forest is a robust, parallelizable variance-reduction method that often works well with little tuning. Gradient-boosted trees usually require more careful tuning but can achieve stronger tabular predictive performance by sequentially correcting the current ensemble.

<details><summary><strong>Expand explanation</strong></summary>

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Comparison

| Property | Random Forest | Gradient Boosting / XGBoost |
|---|---|---|
| Ensemble strategy | Bagging | Boosting |
| Tree training | Largely independent | Sequential |
| Typical trees | Deep | Usually shallower |
| Main mechanism | Average unstable trees | Repeated error correction |
| Parallelism | High across trees | Limited across rounds |
| Tuning sensitivity | Usually lower | Usually higher |
| Noise robustness | Often strong | Can be more sensitive |
| Tabular accuracy | Strong baseline | Often stronger when tuned |

#### When I Would Prefer Random Forest

- I want a strong baseline quickly.
- Tuning budget is small.
- Robustness is more important than squeezing out maximum accuracy.
- Training parallelism matters.
- The dataset is noisy.

#### When I Would Prefer Boosting

- Tabular predictive performance is the priority.
- I can tune and validate carefully.
- There are useful nonlinearities and interactions.
- Sequential corrections continue to improve validation performance.

#### Interview Takeaway

Do not answer:

> "XGBoost is always better."

A stronger answer is:

> Random Forest reduces variance through averaging decorrelated trees, while boosted trees sequentially optimize prediction error. Which wins depends on data size, noise, tuning budget, latency constraints, and the evaluation objective.

:::

</details>
